title: Upgrade (WebSocket) tunnel bypasses max_clients limit and runs without timeout
description: When an HTTP upgrade (e.g., WebSocket) is successfully negotiated, the proxy spawns a detached async task running `copy_bidirectional` to shuttle data between client and backend. This spawned task is completely independent of the connection lifecycle managed by `serve_connection_with_upgrades`. The request counter (`request_count`) is decremented when the outer `serve_connection_with_upgrades` future completes — which happens after the 101 response is sent — but the upgrade tunnel continues running indefinitely in the background. This means upgrade tunnels are not counted against `max_clients`, have no timeout (even when `connection_handling_timeout` is configured), and transfer unlimited data.
impact: An attacker can exhaust server resources (file descriptors, memory, CPU) by opening many WebSocket connections. Each connection frees a `max_clients` slot after the 101 handshake, so the attacker can repeat this to open an unlimited number of concurrent tunnels. Since there is no timeout on the spawned task, idle tunnels persist indefinitely. This enables denial-of-service against the proxy.
attack_path:
1. Attacker sends HTTP/1.1 request with `Connection: upgrade` and `Upgrade: websocket` to a backend that accepts WebSocket.
2. Proxy forwards the upgrade, backend returns 101.
3. Proxy spawns detached `copy_bidirectional` task (handler_main.rs:222) and returns the 101 response.
4. `serve_connection_with_upgrades` completes, `request_count.decrement()` fires (proxy_main.rs:111).
5. Upgrade tunnel runs in the background, not tracked by max_clients.
6. Attacker repeats steps 1-5 to open unlimited concurrent tunnels.
7. Each tunnel holds two OS-level connections (client-side and backend-side) indefinitely.
evidence: rpxy-lib/src/message_handler/handler_main.rs:222 — `self.globals.runtime_handle.spawn(async move { ... copy_bidirectional(...) ... })` spawns a detached task with no timeout and no request tracking
rpxy-lib/src/proxy/proxy_main.rs:77-80 — `request_count.increment()` and max_clients check at connection start
rpxy-lib/src/proxy/proxy_main.rs:111 — `request_count.decrement()` fires when `serve_connection_with_upgrades` returns, before the upgrade tunnel finishes
rpxy-lib/src/proxy/proxy_main.rs:105-108 — `connection_handling_timeout` wraps only `serve_connection_with_upgrades`, not the spawned tunnel task
remediation:
1. Track upgrade tunnels separately in the request counter — increment when the tunnel starts and decrement when `copy_bidirectional` completes.
2. Apply a dedicated `upgrade_tunnel_timeout` to the spawned task (e.g., wrap `copy_bidirectional` in `tokio::time::timeout`).
3. Add idle detection to `copy_bidirectional` (no data transferred for N seconds → close tunnel).
4. Consider a separate `max_upgrade_connections` config limit.

title: 101 Switching Protocols response bypasses response header sanitization
description: When the backend returns a 101 Switching Protocols response, the code path skips `generate_response_forwarded()`, which is responsible for stripping hop-by-hop headers (`Connection`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Proxy-Authenticate`, `Proxy-Authorization`, `Keep-Alive`, etc.), removing the backend's `Server` header, and setting the proxy's own `Server` identifier. The raw 101 response from the backend is forwarded to the client with all original headers intact.
impact: A backend server's 101 response can leak sensitive information to the client: internal server software versions (via `Server` header), proxy authentication challenges (via `Proxy-Authenticate`), internal routing tokens, or other backend-specific headers that would normally be stripped. This exposes internal architecture details to external attackers.
attack_path:
1. Attacker sends a WebSocket upgrade request to a backend that includes verbose headers in its 101 response.
2. Proxy receives the 101 response at handler_main.rs:192.
3. Because `res_backend.status() == StatusCode::SWITCHING_PROTOCOLS`, the code does NOT call `generate_response_forwarded()`.
4. The raw 101 response with all backend headers is returned to the attacker at handler_main.rs:240.
5. Attacker inspects response headers to learn backend server software, internal header conventions, proxy chain details, etc.
evidence: rpxy-lib/src/message_handler/handler_main.rs:192-197 — `generate_response_forwarded` is only called when status != 101; the 101 path at line 200+ skips it entirely
rpxy-lib/src/message_handler/handler_manipulate_messages.rs:22-56 — `generate_response_forwarded` strips hop headers, sets proxy Server header, manages ALT_SVC
remediation: Apply a subset of response header sanitization to 101 responses. At minimum: strip `Proxy-Authenticate`, `Proxy-Authorization`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Keep-Alive`, `Trailer` headers; override the `Server` header with the proxy identifier. Preserve `Connection: Upgrade` and `Upgrade: <protocol>` headers since they are required for the upgrade handshake.

title: No protocol allowlist for HTTP Upgrade — arbitrary protocol tunneling
description: The `extract_upgrade` function accepts any value in the `Upgrade` header without restriction. There is no allowlist of permitted upgrade protocols. The proxy blindly forwards upgrade requests for any protocol (websocket, h2c, IRC, SMTP, or arbitrary custom protocols) to the backend. If the backend accepts the upgrade, a raw bidirectional TCP tunnel is established via `copy_bidirectional` with no protocol-level inspection or filtering.
impact: An attacker can establish raw TCP tunnels through the proxy using any protocol the backend supports. This could be used to: (a) bypass HTTP-level security controls by upgrading to a raw protocol, (b) abuse h2c upgrades to confuse backend request handling, (c) tunnel non-HTTP protocols through the proxy to internal services, (d) leverage the unmonitored tunnel (see finding #1) for long-lived covert channels. Combined with the max_clients bypass, this significantly expands the attack surface.
attack_path:
1. Attacker identifies that the backend supports h2c upgrade (common in development/internal services).
2. Attacker sends: `GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: target\r\nConnection: upgrade\r\nUpgrade: h2c\r\n\r\n`
3. `extract_upgrade` (utils_headers.rs:269) extracts 'h2c' without validation.
4. Proxy strips hop headers, re-inserts `Upgrade: h2c` and `Connection: upgrade` (handler_manipulate_messages.rs:163-167).
5. Request is forwarded to backend; backend responds with 101.
6. `copy_bidirectional` establishes raw tunnel — attacker now speaks HTTP/2 directly to the backend.
7. Attacker can send multiplexed h2 streams to the backend, bypassing any HTTP/1.1 request-level controls the proxy might enforce.
evidence: rpxy-lib/src/message_handler/utils_headers.rs:269-286 — `extract_upgrade` accepts any string value from the Upgrade header with no protocol validation
rpxy-lib/src/message_handler/handler_main.rs:202-203 — protocol match is case-insensitive string comparison only, no allowlist check
remediation:
1. Add a configurable allowlist of permitted upgrade protocols (default: `["websocket"]`).
2. Reject upgrade requests for protocols not in the allowlist with a 400 or 403 response.
3. At minimum, block `h2c` upgrades since HTTP/2 cleartext upgrades bypass HTTP/1.1-level protections and the proxy already handles h2 natively.

title: Connection header only processes first header value — incomplete hop-by-hop header removal
description: The `remove_connection_header` function uses `headers.get(header::CONNECTION)` which returns only the first `Connection` header value. Per RFC 9110 Section 7.6.1, when multiple `Connection` header fields are present, all values must be processed to determine which headers are hop-by-hop. Headers designated as hop-by-hop in subsequent `Connection` header lines are not stripped, causing them to leak through the proxy to the backend (or from backend to client).
impact: An attacker can ensure that certain hop-by-hop designated headers are forwarded through the proxy to the backend by placing the header name in a second `Connection` header line. While the static HOP_HEADERS list covers the most important hop-by-hop headers, any additional headers designated hop-by-hop via the Connection header mechanism (like custom internal headers) would leak if specified in a non-first Connection header line. This can also affect the response path since the same function is used for response headers.
attack_path:
1. Attacker sends a request with two Connection headers:
   `Connection: keep-alive`
   `Connection: x-internal-routing-token`
   `X-Internal-Routing-Token: admin`
2. `remove_connection_header` calls `headers.get(header::CONNECTION)` — returns only `keep-alive`.
3. Only `Keep-Alive` header is removed (if present). `X-Internal-Routing-Token` is NOT removed.
4. `remove_hop_header` removes the static list (`connection`, `te`, `trailer`, etc.) but NOT `x-internal-routing-token`.
5. The backend receives the `X-Internal-Routing-Token: admin` header even though the client declared it as hop-by-hop.
6. If the backend trusts headers from the proxy without re-validating, this can lead to privilege escalation.
evidence: rpxy-lib/src/message_handler/utils_headers.rs:237 — `headers.get(header::CONNECTION)` returns only the first Connection header value, ignoring subsequent ones
rpxy-lib/src/message_handler/utils_headers.rs:238-245 — only the first header value is split and processed
rpxy-lib/src/message_handler/handler_manipulate_messages.rs:24 — same function used during response forwarding
